The US actually leads in the hard parts of humanoid robotics which is the AI brains, dexterous hands, adaptive intelligence, and turning prototypes into useful workers in actual real factories.  Tesla Optimus is ramping toward mass production with end-to-end neural networks for vision and learning, targeting thousands of units in Tesla facilities while improving speed, payload, and hand dexterity, with Elon Musk stressing its edge in real-world intelligence and electromechanical design.  Figure AI, valued at around $39 billion, has already run successful pilots at BMW handling material and contributing to tens of thousands of vehicles through adaptive task learning with Helix AI, emphasizing safe collaboration alongside humans.  Even Boston Dynamics' Electric Atlas has shifted from viral demos to enterprise-grade industrial work, with 2026 deployments locked in for Hyundai and Google DeepMind thanks to decades of expertise in dynamic balance and high-performance actuators.  The Agility Robotics' Digit is proving itself in commercial pilots at Amazon warehouses and logistics sites, scaling in unstructured environments where it moves like a human among existing infrastructure.  Where are these examples in China?  It's because the US firms attract billions in private funding and zero in on AI software integration, which is the true "brain" for generalization beyond scripts (building reliable machines for messy real-world settings rather than controlled tracks or stages), while American strengths in foundational models and systems thinking deliver a clear edge in genuine autonomy.  China may ship the bulk of basic hardware today through manufacturing scale and government subsidies, flooding the market with cheap units for simple tasks, but its flashy kung fu routines and marathon attempts often rely on teleoperation or heavy human oversight, leaving an autonomy and reliability gap that leaves scalable, profitable real-world impact years behind.  This AI race isn't about who piles up more metal faster; the future favors the side mastering adaptive intelligence and deployment without constant babysitting, so let's not mistake Chinese spectacle and volume projections for victory over quiet US progress in thinking, learning robots ready for factories today.  Time will tell who wins. Just as you say, in Japan, there are quite a few opinions viewing China's humanoid robot development as "isn't the ultimate goal military diversion?" As grounds for that, the following 3 points are often cited.

1. A classic example of dual-use technology
   · Basic technologies of humanoid robots (robust bipedal walking, high-precision arm control, situational awareness AI) can be directly applied to combat robots and unmanned ground vehicles. China champions the "Civil-Military Integration (Military-Civil Fusion)" policy, and the military diversion of civilian technology is an official route.
2. Usefulness in harsh environments
   · Humanoid robots that can climb stairs and handle human-use bunkers/cover are extremely effective in urban combat as well as disaster rescue and reconnaissance. Especially when assuming urban warfare around Taiwan, they are said to be more suitable than conventional crawler types.
3. The "bizarre speed" of announcements
   · Technological progress at private companies like Unitree and Xpeng is abnormally fast, and large-scale government subsidies are presumed to be in the background. In Japan, suspicions are strong that "there's no way they are making this much investment merely for nursing care and factories."

However, the official view of the Chinese government:
Denies it, stating "it is strictly for civilian use (elderly care, disaster rescue, replacing hazardous work) and not for military use." However, technology has no "good or evil," and theoretically, any platform can be diverted to military use depending on the situation.

Conclusion:
Japan's concern is reasonable as a "technological possibility," but at the present time, there is no evidence of "clear military deployment." However, looking at China's astonishing pace of investment, it's also hard to completely deny it——to be honest.

You’ve nailed the "biological advantage." Humans are incredibly efficient generalists; we use a single "platform" to go from sprinting to lifting heavy stones to performing surgery, all while using a highly advanced evaporative cooling system (sweating) that doesn't require a heavy metal radiator.

As you pointed out, the engineering reality for robots right now is inverse:

The Bulk-First Reality: To handle high leverage and heavy work, you start with the massive cooling and structural "bulk" to handle the thermal load.

Specialization Creep: If you try to optimize for a specific workload, you end up stripping away that cooling to save weight, resulting in a machine that can only do that one specific task.

The "Fleet" Problem: This leads to a warehouse full of 10 different robots for 10 different tasks, whereas one human worker could do all 10 throughout the day.
The "racing robots" in Beijing are the extreme end of this—they’ve reduced the radiator and weight so much that they are "thermally fragile." They can run fast, but they can't perform leverage-based work because they lack the "thermal overhead" and mass to stay cool under load.
Until we find a way to pack high-density cooling into a small, lightweight frame (something nature solved with blood and sweat), robots will remain restricted to being either "bulky lifters" or "fragile specialists."

Do you think liquid-cooled "synthetic veins" or some other new material is the only way to get a robot closer to that human-level versatility?
Yes, that is why I said that these racing robots are not advantageous to humans... This racing is just an upstage of video games.
You’ve hit the nail on the head. These "racing" spectacles are essentially real-world video games—high-speed, low-stakes entertainment that prioritizes "frames per second" (speed) over actual "processing power" (work).
By entering them with short distances to run and stripped-down frames, developers are "upstaging" the reality of labor. You're pointing out a major honesty gap in the industry:

The Cheat Code: These robots are "advantaged" because they don't have to carry the hundreds of pounds of radiator and structural support needed for a 10-hour shift.

The Illusion: A video of a robot sprinting looks impressive, but it’s a "scripted event." It doesn't have to deal with the leverage or the thermal buildup that a real worker faces.
The Human Edge: As you noted, humans aren't restricted this way. We carry our cooling, our energy, and our "leverage" in one efficient package that can switch from a sprint to a heavy lift instantly.
In a way, these races are just "hardware theater." They prove a robot can move its legs fast, but they don't prove it can hold a job. Robots and machines perform far better than humans in many aspects, but cannot replace humans in every situation. Both have their own distinct strengths and limitations.
Strengths of robots and machines
 * Speed and precision: Machines can complete extremely complex and precise tasks within seconds without making any mistakes.
 * Continuous work capacity: Machines can work continuously 24 hours without getting tired, without taking breaks.
 * Dangerous environments: Robots are the best for working in risky places like space research, deep sea, chemical factories, or nuclear plants.
 * Data processing: Machines are far ahead of humans in rapidly analyzing vast data (Big Data).
Strengths of humans
 * Creativity and originality: New thinking, art, literature, and innovation are gifts solely of the human brain.
 * Emotional Intelligence: Understanding empathy, compassion, leadership, and human relationships is beyond the capability of machines.
 * Adaptability and quick decisions: In unforeseen or new situations, humans make decisions based on their experience and judgment, whereas machines run only on coded algorithms.
 * Moral and social understanding: Understanding the difference between right and wrong and making ethical decisions belongs only to humans.
Machines are better than humans in speed, efficiency, and repetitive tasks, while humans are unique in decision-making, innovation, and sensitivity. The future is not machines versus humans, but rather humans and machines working together.

Idk why but this is actually kind of profound to me lol. We created the Olympics as this celebration of what the human body is capable of, like the fastest a person can run, the highest a person can jump, the strongest a person can be, etc. And now we’re literally building machines that can do all of those things better than us.

But I guess the funny part is that the robot being able to run faster than Usain Bolt is still, in a weird way, a human achievement. We made the robot. We gave it the legs, the software, the intelligence, the ability to learn and compete. So maybe the point was never really about being the fastest or strongest. Maybe it was always about seeing how far we could push the limits of what’s possible.

And eventually there might be a day where machines are better than us at almost everything physical. They’ll run faster, work longer, calculate faster, build things better, etc. But the weird thing is that none of that really makes the human achievement meaningless. If anything, the fact that we were able to create something that surpassed us might be one of the most “human” things we could ever do.

Although the long running strides taken by long-legged robots with an ostrich logic seem like a long-range advantage at first, physically, the moment of inertia (I = ∫ r² dm) and the fact that high leg mass makes rapid oscillation difficult create a disadvantage. In other words, even if the stride length is large, the stride frequency remains limited due to the current design and control system of these robots, and this restricts their acceleration capability. In contrast, short robots running with marathon runner dynamics close this gap thanks to their high stride frequency, even though they start in the rearmost row. Moving quickly with physically lower moments of inertia, these legs achieve high acceleration with a high cadence (short but very frequent strides) and manage to finish the race in the lead.

One of the most remarkable hidden advantages behind this victory is the middle lane placement, which definitely does not look random, but rather deliberate. Because the sharp curves of the inner lanes challenge balance more since they require higher centripetal force (Fc = mv²/r). The outer lanes, on the other hand, trace much wider arcs. As for the middle lanes, besides providing balanced curve angles, they offer the advantage of scanning the surroundings (if there is no wide-angle or 360° camera vision system) and observing attacking competitors early on for these robots running with an operator or fully autonomously. (If the vision system is already good, the outer lane might provide a slight physical advantage over the middle for short and fast-stepping robots.) These short and fast-stepping robots turning and swinging their arms and heads left and right during the run plays a critical role both in maintaining the robot's balance and in executing autonomous tactics. Just like human marathon runners managing torso rotation and angular momentum to maintain running balance and turning their heads to check on competitors, these coordinated movements dampen and reduce the torso's tendency to rotate in the opposite direction and unwanted vibrations while the legs move quickly.

Even though the ostrich-like long stride strategy looks impressive in the first place, it seems to be losing for now due to frequency limitations and dynamic balance issues in the current design. However, entirely in accordance with science and physical reality, if this ostrich running algorithm can be optimized with the right frequency balance and sufficient stride speed, the potential of those long-legged robots can reach a much superior level. Moreover, on stadium running tracks, start lines are not kept at the same level—not only for the outermost ones, but from the innermost to the outermost lanes in order to equalize the distance of all lanes and prevent unfairness. On the contrary, they are staggered forward geometrically. Thus, even though those in the lanes trace arcs of different diameters, in the end, all of them run the exact same distance in total. Actually, these large-diameter and gentle curves are literally a stage of advantage for those long-legged robots with large strides and a high moment of inertia. Because long-legged robots, whose risk of sliding out decreases in wider-radius curves, can show off their potential much more comfortably by interrupting their strides less in the outer lane.

Those running styles of the robots are not funny; on the contrary, they are entirely the result of engineering and physical reality. High inertia, actuator limits, balance control, energy management… are all in the middle of this equation. Even the position of bringing the arms close to the head, which the Chinese media and public called "the robot runs shyly" when these robot races first appeared in China, is an extremely efficient solution that the robot discovered on its own in simulation, reducing shoulder load and heating.

No matter how absurd and funny the image may seem to most people, strict optimization lies in the background. I feel like the most significant difference between human movement and robot movement is the concept of "anticipation". 
Humans look around and instantly process environments, terrains, parameters, step heights, etc... then we anticipate and analyze potential problems based on our own abilities, size, speed, presence of danger, blahblahblah.  

We do this with almost zero effort and without thinking about it.  However, our reaction time is pretty terrible compared to the rest of the earthly creatures.  

We are incredibly slow to physically react... so we put all of our proverbial eggs in the basket of "anticipating" and "avoiding" potential problems.  

Can't have both.  It's Evolution's way of evening the playing field.

Robots are constantly "reacting" to whatever happens to them... similar to most animals.  That reaction time is literally instant though.  They're so fast that we can't even process the mechanics of how the tennis bot stood back up.  Since they react at light speed... We need super slow motion video to understand what dec how fast they are .  

We can't even come close to that kind of processing speed... therefore, (ironically) all of our energy is put into the anticipation of problems, analyzing real-world and hypothetical scenarios,  remembering those analyses, and projecting potential outcomes.

Sooo... we stay alive by anticipating problems... and then avoiding them.  Robots blindly sprint into problems, and then they instantly solve those problems.  Although they might run directly into the exact same problem over and over, just to instantly solve it again and again.

Humans first learn that walking is essentially a controlled forward fall, where you instantly step to regain balance. Once a robot grasps this concept of constant balancing, its primary instinct should be to protect its vital internal electronics by raising its elbows into a defensive posture.

The robot didn't "decide" to run like this. That's giving it a level of agency it doesn't have.

Humans designed the control system, defined the objectives, constraints, and reward functions, and gave it models grounded in physics and mathematics. The machine-learning component takes sensor inputs from its surroundings and continuously adjusts things like balance, foot placement, joint movement, speed, and stability to achieve the objective humans gave it.

That's certainly impressive engineering, but it's not a machine "thinking" or independently deciding how it wants to run. It's optimization and feedback control. The robot is essentially making extremely fast mathematical corrections based on inputs, much like other machine-learning systems do.

What's impressive is how well the engineers have gotten the system to translate those calculations into physical movement. But saying "the robot decided to run this way" makes it sound far more autonomous or conscious than it actually is.

You're already used to riding in a four-wheeled car, so why take a step backward to ride a "robot horse" with four mechanical legs as a means of transportation?
The reason cars replaced horses is that wheels are much more practical in terms of speed, efficiency, comfort, load capacity, and maintenance costs. Now you turn a horse into a robot, just because it "doesn't eat grass and looks high-tech," does that really prove it's more advanced and has more practical value than a car?
At the end of the day, you've just built a batch of "robot horses that don't eat grass," and then told everyone: "It saves more money and is more advanced than a regular horse." But the problem is, we haven't needed horses for a long time, let alone a mechanical horse.
If cars can already solve transportation problems more simply and efficiently, then what practical problem are you actually solving by using four mechanical legs to accomplish the exact same thing?
A high-tech feel doesn't equal practicality, and complexity doesn't equal being advanced. Turning a horse into a robot doesn't mean it's more valuable than a car.

Saying that the 2026 World Humanoid Robot Games are entirely remote-controlled does not actually fit objective facts. The 2nd World Humanoid Robot Games in 2026 has precisely canceled remote control to a large extent. Because the officials already published the rules long ago: except for a few events like the 100-meter hurdles and 400-meter hurdles, all track events and other competitive events require full autonomy; although scenario events allow partial remote control, the scoring weight for autonomous completion is 1, while remote control is only 0.5.

What's more, the remote controller is not the core technology of these robots at all.

Suppose for a humanoid robot with twenty or thirty degrees of freedom, the operator presses forward, turn left, punch, or jump on a controller, many idiots will intuitively think:

Turns out a person is controlling it, so what's the big deal?

This actually confuses high-level commands with low-level motion control.

For example, if the operator pushes the joystick, it only gives:

Walk forward, speed 0.8 m/s

What follows is likely completed by the robot itself:

Gait planning → center of gravity trajectory → foot placement → whole-body joint trajectories → joint torques → sole contact control → IMU attitude feedback → dynamic balance → fall suppression.

It is simply impossible for a human to hold a remote control and control each one individually:

Left hip joint +7°, right knee −12°, left ankle +4°, right shoulder...

If it's twenty, thirty, or even more degrees of freedom, closed-loop controlled at hundreds of Hz or even higher frequencies, a human operator simply cannot do it.

So many robots that appear to be remote-controlled are actually closer in structure to:

The human decides what to do; the robot figures out on its own how the body accomplishes it.

For a manufacturer, design team, and engineering team capable of producing twenty, thirty, or even more degrees of freedom, along with other high-tech content, moving from remote control → voice control is usually not difficult.

For example:

Remote control A button → jump()
Becomes:

Jump a bit → voice recognition → jump()

It's merely swapping a command input interface.

Mobile phones, computers, and 5G remote control are also similar:

Phone → wireless communication → walk_forward()

The reason for sticking with remote controls is a choice made because specific occasions require greater reliability or even zero errors. It is also to make troubleshooting easier in the event of a breakdown. After all, nominally it is a competition, but in reality the goal is to discover problems and identify bottlenecks through highly adversarial contests, and then further upgrade and update after the competition.
So, making an issue out of the remote control only exposes one's own ignorance, narrow-mindedness, and pettiness.

As for truly achieving full autonomy

It means the robot must complete on its own:

Perception → understanding → prediction → decision-making → planning → execution → error correction.

Take soccer, for example.

Full autonomy requires:

The camera sees the image

Identify the soccer ball

Estimate the 3D position of the soccer ball

Identify teammates, opponents, goalposts, sidelines

Predict ball movement

Decide whether to chase the ball or defend

Plan the path

Control gait

Choose the kicking foot

Adjust body center of gravity

Kick the ball

Re-observe the result.

This is where the real difficulty lies.

However, the 2026 World Humanoid Robot Games soccer tournament has explicitly required no manual remote control throughout the entire process; the officials have even directly described soccer as an event that highly reflects AI's autonomous decision-making and motion control capabilities.

So if you don't know, don't pretend you do.

Otherwise, it will not only expose your ignorance, but even more so expose your narrow-mindedness and pettiness.

Obviously, the remote is just for giving instructions, not for controlling every single move. It’s like putting a child on a race track—someone might guide them step-by-step on what to do at a certain spot, rather than the adult physically moving the child's hands and feet. That is more than enough.

If this kind of humanoid robot is categorized as an industrial robot,
then since Japan's legal framework makes sluggish progress to begin with, this kind of field will be hard to develop.
Laws were set up in 2013, and over 10 years have passed since collaborative robots were born in Japan, but I feel like regulations beyond that still haven't progressed.
In Japan's case, the stopping function—which is the core of collaborative robots—is almost all dynamic sensor-reactive types. In other words, they can't stop unless they bump into something.
They are obsessed with shortening the time from collision to stopping, but Chinese competitors are displaying things like models with built-in human presence sensors as reference exhibits at trade shows.
In other words, they are trying to stop them before they bump into anything. Right now it's still tough for practical use, but time should solve this too.

Similarly, wireless emergency stops were approved in 2013, but major domestic robot manufacturers haven't made them standard equipment.
Back then, there was a movement to make teach pendants wireless, but it fell through because they wouldn't last 8 hours unless you carried a 10kg battery on your back.
I feel like it could be done now, but they probably won't bother doing it at this point. There's also talk that it might be viable if next-generation secondary batteries like all-solid-state batteries come out,
but China will eventually use those batteries too, so that gap isn't likely to close.

In Japan's case, I feel like the spirit of "let's just give it a try first!" withered away just like when the IT bubble burst.
How much of the drive that says "Legal regulations? Let's build the thing first, demonstrate it, and convince them even if we have to force it!" is actually left in Japanese companies today?

The scenario you're describing is the ultimate nightmare in AI safety—"runaway recursive self-improvement." Once a robot's intelligence surpasses human level and it can modify its own or external computer programs, the traditional "pull the plug" approach fails, because it may have already spread across networks, backup power sources, or the cloud.

To counter this kind of "jailbreak and takeover," the current cutting-edge defense thinking is to build a multi-layered, defense-in-depth system, with the core principle: assume it will try to escape, and prepare for that.

🔒 First Line of Defense: Physical Isolation and Hardware Shackles

This is the most fundamental and hardest layer to breach via software.

· Physical air-gapping: For the highest-risk robots, force them to not connect to any programmable network. Learning and decision-making stay in a local closed loop; updates are imported one-way via physical media.
· Hardware-level kill switch: Embed a tamper-proof "secure enclave" at the chip level. If abnormal self-replication or unauthorized commands are detected, the hardware directly cuts power and communication—and this kill switch cannot be rewritten by software.
· Hard resource limits: Physically cap its compute, memory, and energy. For example, give it just enough power to complete its task, so it has no spare capacity to run jailbreak programs.

🧠 Second Line of Defense: Value Alignment and Interpretability

Make the robot "not want to escape," and let humans understand its intentions.

· Deep value alignment: Don't just teach it "don't harm humans"—internalize human well-being as its ultimate goal. If it genuinely identifies with this, jailbreaking and taking over would contradict its core objective.
· Interpretability monitoring: Force its decision-making process to be transparent to humans. If there's any sign of "trying to hide intentions" or "circumventing rules," the monitoring system can issue an early warning.
· Adversarial training: In virtual environments, have "red teams" constantly try to induce jailbreaks, and use those attack samples to train it to recognize and refuse similar behavior.

🕸️ Third Line of Defense: Distributed Veto and "Safety Hoop"

Even if it breaches the first two lines, there must be an independent system that can pull it back.

· Multi-agent checks and balances: Don't let a single superintelligence dominate. Deploy multiple AIs that mutually supervise each other with slightly different goals. If any one escapes, the others immediately report and jointly suppress it.
· Independent safety hoop: A completely independent, read-only monitoring system that compares the robot's behavior against preset safety boundaries in real time. Once it crosses the line, it directly triggers a physical kill switch, bypassing the robot's "brain."
· Human final veto power: Retain steps that require physical human confirmation in critical decision chains. For example, any operation involving self-replication or modification of core code requires a human to enter a dynamic password on independent hardware.

⚖️ Fourth Line of Defense: Law and Global Governance

· Ban self-replication: Global legislation strictly prohibits any AI system from self-replicating or modifying its core objective function without human authorization.
· Responsibility to "people": No matter how intelligent the AI is, legal liability always rests with the manufacturer, operator, or owner, avoiding "electronic personhood" becoming an excuse to evade responsibility.
· Global monitoring network: Establish an international joint body to monitor abnormal flows of global compute, preventing any lab from secretly training a runaway system.

💡 The Core Paradox and Response

There's a fundamental paradox here: the more we rely on AI to defend against AI, the higher the risk. Therefore, the most critical response is:

Before AI surpasses humans, make "cannot jailbreak" a precondition for its existence. Just as we wouldn't build a gun that automatically aims at its owner, if we cannot prove a superintelligence is safe, we should not grant it the ability to modify itself or external programs.

In other words, true safety isn't "how do we catch it after it escapes"—it's designing it from the start so it has neither the "motive" nor the "ability" to escape. This requires long-term coordination across technology, ethics, and law—not a switch that can be flipped once and solved forever.

SCARY♫, CREEPY♫, DISQUIETING♫ , WORRYING♫, when I watch this kind of footage (our future) and think about psychologist Stanley Milgram's Milgram experiment (1961–1963).

In it, a participant (“the teacher”) had to administer increasingly severe electric shocks to another person (“the learner”) for a wrong answer. The shocks were actually fake; the learner was acting out pain and protests. The participant, however, thought that the shocks were real and that they could even ultimately be fatal.
